1.B: Wilms tumour arises within the kidney, rarely calcifies and rarely crosses the midline; it does not raise urinary catecholamine metabolites.
1.C: Adrenocortical carcinoma is adrenal but presents with virilisation or Cushing features from steroid excess, not raised VMA/HVA with calcification crossing the midline.
1.D: Hepatoblastoma is a liver mass marked by raised AFP, not an adrenal mass with urinary catecholamine metabolites.

2.A: Neuroblastoma is usually suprarenal, often crosses the midline, calcifies and makes the child look unwell; a painless intrarenal mass in a well 3-year-old favours Wilms.
2.B: Renal cell carcinoma is a tumour of adolescents and adults; in a 3-year-old a renal mass is far more likely to be Wilms.
2.C: Rhabdomyosarcoma usually arises in the head and neck, genitourinary tract or extremities, not as a primary renal mass with hypertension.

3.A: Leukocoria is not conjunctivitis; antibiotic drops only delay diagnosis of retinoblastoma or another sight-threatening cause.
3.B: Observation risks loss of the eye, extraocular spread and death from retinoblastoma; leukocoria needs urgent assessment.
3.D: A six-month routine review is far too late; leukocoria with strabismus needs urgent dilated fundus examination.

4.A: Biliary atresia presents with cholestatic jaundice and pale stools in early infancy, not a large liver mass with markedly raised AFP.
4.C: Infantile hepatic haemangioma is a vascular lesion of early infancy without marked AFP elevation beyond the age-expected range.
4.D: Focal nodular hyperplasia is a benign lesion, usually in older children, with normal AFP.

5.B: Ewing sarcoma favours the diaphysis with an onion-skin reaction and soft-tissue mass; a metaphyseal distal femur lesion with sunburst reaction favours osteosarcoma.
5.C: Osteomyelitis gives fever and periosteal new bone but not a destructive sunburst pattern of tumour osteoid in a teenager with progressive pain.
5.D: Chondroblastoma is a benign epiphyseal lesion, not an aggressive metaphyseal tumour with sunburst periosteal reaction.

6.A: Osteosarcoma typically involves the metaphysis with a sunburst reaction; a diaphyseal onion-skin lesion with fever is classic for Ewing.
6.B: Giant cell tumour is an epiphyseal lesion of skeletally mature young adults, without fever or onion-skin periosteal reaction.
6.C: Osteochondroma is a benign exostosis projecting from the metaphysis, not a painful febrile diaphyseal lesion.

7.A: Wilms tumour is a renal tumour and does not present as a primary orbital mass.
7.B: Hepatoblastoma is a liver tumour; it is not an orbital soft-tissue sarcoma.
7.D: Osteosarcoma is a bone tumour of long-bone metaphyses, not a rapidly growing orbital soft-tissue mass.

8.A: Fanconi syndrome causes hypokalaemia and hypophosphataemia from proximal tubular losses, the opposite of this pattern.
8.C: SIADH causes hyponatraemia with concentrated urine, not hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia.
8.D: Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and hypernatraemia, not the potassium, phosphate and calcium pattern of cell lysis.

9.B: Waiting for culture positivity delays treatment by hours to days; febrile neutropenia mortality rises with every hour without antibiotics.
9.C: Antipyretic alone with discharge ignores a potentially fatal bacteraemia; febrile neutropenia needs assessment and empiric IV antibiotics.
9.D: Deferring assessment until morning breaches the time-to-antibiotic standard, usually within about an hour of presentation.

10.A: Physiotherapy without imaging misses cord compression, where delay causes permanent paralysis and sphincter loss.
10.B: New weakness and urinary retention in a child with cancer are red flags; reassurance and discharge is unsafe.
10.C: Neurological outcome depends on function when treatment starts; imaging must be urgent (MRI spine), not delayed for two weeks.

11.A: Supine positioning lets the mass compress the trachea and great vessels, precipitating airway or cardiovascular collapse.
11.B: Sedation reduces airway tone and spontaneous effort and can cause collapse; it is unsafe in clinic with stridor and orthopnoea.
11.D: General anaesthesia with loss of spontaneous ventilation can cause complete obstruction; it needs expert multidisciplinary planning, never an unplanned elective approach.

12.A: Favourable histology (INPC/Shimada) is a good prognostic feature, not an adverse one.
12.C: Age under 18 months is a favourable factor in neuroblastoma, not adverse.
12.D: Localised disease is favourable; extent alone does not denote high risk the way MYCN amplification does.

13.B: Turner syndrome is associated with horseshoe kidney but is not a classic Wilms predisposition syndrome like WAGR.
13.C: Marfan syndrome is a fibrillin-1 connective tissue disorder without Wilms tumour predisposition.
13.D: Noonan syndrome predisposes to JMML and some other tumours, not specifically Wilms tumour as WAGR (WT1 deletion) does.

14.A: Infection does not produce multifocal bilateral retinal tumours; bilaterality reflects a germline RB1 mutation.
14.B: Trauma does not cause retinoblastoma; bilateral multifocal tumours indicate heritable disease.
14.C: Vitamin A deficiency causes xerophthalmia and keratomalacia, not retinoblastoma.

15.A: Turner syndrome is not a recognised hepatoblastoma predisposition; the classic associations are BWS, FAP and extreme prematurity.
15.B: Achondroplasia (FGFR3) does not carry an increased hepatoblastoma risk.
15.D: Cystic fibrosis causes liver disease but is not a hepatoblastoma predisposition; overgrowth syndromes such as BWS are.

16.A: Radiotherapy before histology risks treating the wrong disease and is not standard; tissue diagnosis comes first.
16.C: Excision without staging or diagnosis contaminates margins and compromises limb-salvage and curative surgery.
16.D: A poorly placed biopsy tract seeds tumour and may force amputation; the tract must be excisable at definitive surgery.

17.B: 5-HIAA is a serotonin metabolite used for carcinoid tumours, not neuroblastoma.
17.C: Urinary cortisol assesses Cushing syndrome or adrenocortical tumours, not catecholamine-secreting neural crest tumours.
17.D: Urinary glucose has no role in diagnosing neuroblastoma.

18.A: Neuroblastoma typically arises outside the kidney and encases rather than displaces major vessels.
18.B: Adrenal lymphoma is rare in children and is suprarenal, not an intrarenal mass displacing vessels.
18.C: Phaeochromocytoma is an adrenal medullary tumour, not intrarenal, and presents with paroxysmal catecholamine symptoms.

19.A: Fundus examination uses no radiation and is essential for diagnosis and follow-up.
19.B: Ocular ultrasound uses no ionising radiation and helps show calcification, so it need not be avoided.
19.D: MRI is the preferred cross-sectional modality precisely because it avoids radiation in germline RB1 carriers.

20.A: High-risk patients need close laboratory monitoring to detect TLS early; omitting it is unsafe.
20.C: Potassium supplementation worsens TLS hyperkalaemia; potassium is withheld from hydration fluids.
20.D: Routine calcium loading can precipitate calcium-phosphate deposition; calcium is reserved for symptomatic hypocalcaemia or arrhythmia.

21.B: Oral iron has no role in hyperkalaemia and does not stabilise the myocardium.
21.C: IV phosphate would worsen TLS hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia.
21.D: Oral bicarbonate shifts potassium slowly and modestly, does not stabilise the myocardium, and alkalinisation may worsen calcium-phosphate precipitation.

22.A: Temperature alone does not separate low from high risk; ANC, clinical stability, comorbidities and treatment context matter.
22.B: Child preference may inform outpatient options but cannot determine safe disposition.
22.C: A single normal blood pressure does not exclude early sepsis; validated risk stratification is needed.

23.A: AFP is a germ-cell tumour and hepatoblastoma marker, not diagnostic of lymphoma.
23.B: A chest radiograph helps assess mediastinal involvement but cannot give a histological diagnosis.
23.D: Empiric treatment without tissue risks missing the subtype and can obscure the diagnosis, especially with steroids.

24.A: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma is rare in children and presents with skin lesions, not a rapidly enlarging abdominal mass.
24.C: Follicular lymphoma is indolent with slow growth, the opposite of very high cell turnover.
24.D: Hodgkin lymphoma usually presents with cervical or mediastinal nodes and is not a rapidly enlarging high-turnover abdominal mass.

25.B: Urinary catecholamines are a neuroblastoma test with no role in ALL CNS staging.
25.C: Serum AFP is a marker for hepatoblastoma and germ-cell tumours, not CNS leukaemia.
25.D: Skull radiographs cannot detect leptomeningeal leukaemia; CNS status is defined by CSF cell count and cytology.

26.A: Chronic-phase CML presents with splenomegaly and leucocytosis with maturing myeloid cells, not gum and skin infiltration by blasts.
26.B: Hairy cell leukaemia is an adult disease with pancytopenia and splenomegaly, not paediatric gingival infiltration.
26.C: Pure red cell aplasia is isolated erythroid failure without blasts or tissue infiltration.

27.A: Platelets are not contraindicated in APL; aggressive platelet, plasma and cryoprecipitate support is given to correct the coagulopathy.
27.B: APL with coagulopathy is a haemorrhagic emergency needing admission, not outpatient follow-up.
27.D: Early haemorrhagic deaths occur in the first days; ATRA should start on suspicion without waiting for PML-RARA confirmation.

28.A: Bone age is assessed on a hand radiograph and has no relation to MRD.
28.C: Blood group compatibility is a transfusion test, not a measure of leukaemic response.
28.D: Renal function is assessed with creatinine and electrolytes; MRD measures residual leukaemic cells.

29.B: Constipation does not explain fever and bowel-wall thickening in a neutropenic child.
29.C: Lactose intolerance causes bloating and diarrhoea without fever or bowel-wall thickening.
29.D: Intussusception shows a target sign and is not present in all cases; neutropenic fever with bowel-wall thickening fits typhlitis.

30.A: Avoiding cultures loses the chance to identify the organism and a catheter-related bloodstream infection.
30.B: Stool culture alone misses bacteraemia, the main concern with a central line and neutropenic fever.
30.C: Urine dipstick alone is insufficient; neutropenic children may lack pyuria, and blood cultures are essential.
